children.author: theseamusjames
children.text:
I did this a few months ago and it's not simple: different sensors have different pixel arrangements, files can have different data structures, and the default tone mapping is provided by the app (so opening the same raw file in darktable vs preview will have different results). There are different algorithms for how you assemble the raw data as well, and the issue is that you can get something _passable_ that isn't _optimal_, and it's really hard for the LLM to recognize that something isn't right. Is it the pixel processing, or is it the tone mapping, or is that just how the image looked?

And on top of that, you need a bunch of different files from different sensors to test with. Canon, sony, apple, fuji, nikon, olympus, etc. -- if you're building a truly general application, that's a concern.

Or if you're like me and you shoot fuji, you just build a fuji raw parser and call it good. The "TAM of 1" world of software development...
That's exactly what I was thinking. It's only a matter of time. Surely the models, when well directed, can get most or all of the way there in short order.

children.text:
Yeah, it's a really well defined problem space with quantifiable outcomes, so LLMs are very well suited to it.

For lopsy, the biggest issue I ran into was combinatorial bugs: certain sequences of tools and actions would cause a bug to occur that wasn't obvious from isolated tool testing. I solved it by having Claude generate complete projects, full documents with novel concepts chosen randomly, built in the browser with playwright. This continues to expose so much more than individual unit/tool tests, and I have an automated loop that addresses them. (And a bonus from that: I use the outputs to make tutorials to show what the tool can do).

How many painting applications have been built by LLMs I wonder?

I also let it build one btw: https://egeozcan.github.io/ketchup/ (not a PS clone, more amateur painting oriented)

I also built one of these photoshop clones. It has raw support. I use it for Fuji raw editing. I've been building it with Claude for 6 months now.

Just try loading a RAW photo into Lightroom/Photoshop and put the window next to Lightcraft/Photocraft - the results are completely different and not in a good way. Lightcraft's image looks like an amateur attempt at RAW processing from first principles, without any of the most basic colour profiles and adjustments that Lightroom applies. I'd treat this as completely new, far from complete software heavily inspired by the Adobe Suite, rather than a "port".

But maybe folks who use workflows that don't involve RAW photos have better luck.

children.text: Because there are only 24 hours in a day, and you have other problems you want to solve. It comes down to data interchange. What does your business have as inputs, and what does it have has outputs? For some, it's emails with PDF attachments, others it's an API accessible via http. Others it's raw ingredients and the output is food. Sometimes you go to a restaurant and pay someone else to do the cooking. Other times, you cook yourself.

In this hypothetical future, why would I (or my business) buy software from any company, when I can just prompt the equivalent into existence myself? Post AI - What is the future of making money with software? Desktop apps or SaaS? This certainly also would cut into the bottom line of software companies so they won't exist and then these companies are supposed to be the prime customers of the AI companies.

children.author: pcglue
children.text:
I was able to use Photocraft and Claude to do something that the plain generative image AI in ChatGPT couldn't. I had two photos of the same location, one with 3 people, one with 1 person. I took the photos with the people strategically standing where the photos could be easily be combined without the people interfering with one another. A month ago, I tried using ChatGPT to combine the people into one photo. Its attempts never looked right. It always changed the faces of everyone. Today, I tried using Claude and this Photocraft MCP server to do this. After 3 quick tries over 5 minutes, it did it. The 2 additional tries were to have it fix some lighting differences. Thanks to the person who created this!

Yes, I could have definitely done it myself, but that's besides the point. It wasn't important/urgent enough for me to spend 20-30 minutes to do it (yet). But I was curious enough to play with this to have it done this way.
